author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the major structural components of DNA, including sugar-phosphate backbones, nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds, and relate them to the double-helix architecture.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules and hydrogen-bond counts to determine the sequence of a complementary DNA strand.
Explain why DNA strands are antiparallel by referencing 5' and 3' directionality of the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Describe the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase during DNA replication.
Compare leading- and lagging-strand synthesis and explain why Okazaki fragments arise on one daughter strand.
Predict daughter-molecule composition after one and two rounds of DNA replication and justify why replication is semiconservative.

modules.description: A schematic ladder representation introduces DNA backbones, bases, and complementary pairing before students encounter the twisted helix.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recognize DNA as two repeating sugar-phosphate backbones connected by paired bases.
Identify the four nitrogenous bases by label and color.
Interpret each rung as a complementary base pair linking the two strands.
instructions: Observe the flat ladder model from the front.
Use Next and Previous to compare the labels and color coding on each rung.

components.text: A red | T blue | G yellow | C green

clips.changeMeaning: The schematic ladder and title are presented as the first simplified representation so students can focus on repeating DNA structure without helical geometry.
clips.narration: DNA can first be understood as a regular ladder-like polymer. The two side rails represent repeating sugar-phosphate backbones, and the horizontal rungs represent paired nitrogenous bases.

clips.changeMeaning: Backbone labels and a color legend appear to direct attention to the repeating rails and the four base identities that form the interior of the molecule.
clips.narration: Each strand contains a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside. The bases project inward, where adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine pair across the ladder.

clips.changeMeaning: A bond overlay appears across selected rungs so learners can see that each rung represents a specific complementary base pair rather than a generic connection.
clips.narration: The pattern is specific: adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine. This complementary arrangement is what allows one strand to determine the sequence of the other.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: From Ladder to Double Helix
modules.description: The flat ladder transitions into a realistic DNA double helix, helping students map schematic features onto 3D structure.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate the ladder model to the 3D double helix.
Recognize that the backbones spiral around a common axis while bases stack inside.
Observe that one full helical turn spans about ten base pairs.
instructions: Watch the ladder twist into a helix.
Compare the schematic and realistic forms as the narration explains how they map onto one another.

clips.changeMeaning: A side-by-side comparison appears so learners can directly map the flat schematic onto the realistic three-dimensional double helix representation.
clips.narration: The ladder model is useful, but real DNA is twisted. Here the same backbones and base pairs are shown in the three-dimensional double-helix form found in cells.

clips.changeMeaning: The helix is enlarged and slightly rotated while a turn label appears, emphasizing spiral geometry and the approximate periodicity of one full turn per ten base pairs.
clips.narration: The sugar-phosphate backbones spiral around a common axis, while the base pairs stack in the interior. A full turn of the helix spans roughly ten base pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: The two models move closer together and the helix rotates further, helping students mentally align the corresponding parts across schematic and realistic representations.
clips.narration: You can compare schematic and realistic views. Notice that the side rails of the ladder become the outer spiraling backbones, and the rungs become stacked base pairs inside the helix.

modules.description: Directional arrows and 5' and 3' labels show that the two DNA strands run in opposite directions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define the 5' and 3' directionality of a DNA strand.
Explain what it means for two DNA strands to be antiparallel.
Relate antiparallel orientation to the chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone.
instructions: Rotate the helix mentally as the arrows appear.
Pay attention to the end labels on each strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Directional arrows are added directly on the helix to show that the two strands point in opposite directions along the backbone.
clips.narration: DNA strands are directional. One backbone runs in one chemical direction, while the complementary backbone runs in the opposite direction.

clips.changeMeaning: The strand ends are labeled 5' and 3' so students can connect the arrows to the named termini of each backbone.
clips.narration: These ends are named 5-prime and 3-prime, referring to carbons in the sugar. One strand runs 5-prime to 3-prime, and the other runs 3-prime to 5-prime.

clips.changeMeaning: The helix is enlarged and rotated to emphasize that opposite strand orientation is a structural requirement imposed by backbone chemistry, not a decorative convention.
clips.narration: This opposite orientation is called antiparallel. It is not optional: the directional chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone forces the two strands to run in opposite directions.

modules.description: Students conceptually complete a missing strand by applying base-pairing rules and observing hydrogen-bond counts.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Use A-T and G-C pairing rules to infer a complementary strand.
Associate A-T with two hydrogen bonds and G-C with three.
Recognize that the newly completed strand is antiparallel to the template strand.
instructions: Imagine dragging bases from the palette to the empty strand.
Watch which placements are accepted and how hydrogen bonds appear.

clips.changeMeaning: A template strand, empty complementary positions, and a base palette appear to frame the complementary-pairing problem visually.
clips.narration: Here the left strand is given, and the right strand is missing its bases. Use the pairing rules to determine which bases belong opposite each template base.

clips.changeMeaning: A feedback label appears and the ladder shifts slightly upward, signaling that correct complements are being placed and accepted by the activity.
clips.narration: Correct pairs snap into position: adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine. If a base does not complement the template, the system rejects it because the bonding pattern is wrong.

clips.changeMeaning: Dashed hydrogen-bond overlays appear across the paired bases to make invisible intermolecular interactions visible for comparison between pair types.
clips.narration: When a correct pair forms, hydrogen bonds hold the bases together. Adenine-thymine pairs form two hydrogen bonds, while guanine-cytosine pairs form three.

clips.changeMeaning: The full complementary sequence is revealed and labeled in the opposite direction, tying pairing accuracy to antiparallel strand orientation.
clips.narration: The completed complementary strand is 3-prime to 5-prime relative to the template shown as 5-prime to 3-prime. Complementary pairing and antiparallel directionality always go together in double-stranded DNA.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5: Helicase Opens the Double Helix
modules.description: Helicase appears and unwinds the DNA to create the initial replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase as the enzyme that opens the double helix.
Describe unwinding as the breaking of hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
Recognize the replication fork as the region where strands separate.
instructions: Follow the helicase as it moves along the DNA.
Notice how the fork opens behind the enzyme.

clips.changeMeaning: The replication scene begins with helicase positioned at one end of the helix so students can identify the first enzyme entering the process.
clips.narration: Replication starts by opening the double helix. Helicase binds at the DNA and begins moving along it to separate the two parental strands.

clips.changeMeaning: Helicase advances, the fork region visibly widens, and broken-bond overlays appear so strand separation becomes observable as a progressive process.
clips.narration: As helicase moves forward, it breaks the hydrogen bonds between paired bases. The strands unwind and a replication fork forms behind the enzyme.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Single-Strand Binding Proteins Stabilize DNA
modules.description: SSBs bind exposed DNA behind helicase to keep the separated strands open and stable.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify single-strand binding proteins on exposed DNA.
Explain why separated single strands need stabilization.
Relate SSB binding to maintaining an open replication fork.
instructions: Look just behind helicase to see where stabilizing proteins bind.
Compare the exposed strands before and after SSB binding.

clips.changeMeaning: Stabilizing proteins appear on both exposed templates just behind the opened fork, emphasizing their role after unwinding rather than before it.
clips.narration: Once helicase opens the DNA, single-strand binding proteins attach to the exposed strands. They keep the separated templates from re-pairing or folding back on themselves.

clips.changeMeaning: The SSB clusters spread along the exposed strands, visually reinforcing that stabilization extends over the unwound region of single-stranded DNA.
clips.narration: These proteins coat the single strands and hold them open. By stabilizing the templates, they make the DNA accessible for the enzymes that synthesize new strands.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7: DNA Polymerase and the Leading Strand
modules.description: DNA polymerase continuously synthesizes the leading strand in the same overall direction as fork movement.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify DNA polymerase as the enzyme that adds nucleotides to a growing strand.
Explain that synthesis always proceeds 5' to 3'.
Describe why one daughter strand can be synthesized continuously at the fork.
instructions: Track the polymerase on the template that supports continuous synthesis.
Watch free nucleotides join the growing daughter strand.

clips.changeMeaning: DNA polymerase and a pool of nucleotides are added to one template strand to introduce continuous daughter-strand synthesis at the fork.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase builds a new strand by adding nucleotides to a 3-prime end. That means the new strand always grows in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.

clips.changeMeaning: The polymerase advances with the fork while a continuous daughter strand grows visibly behind it, directly showing why this template supports uninterrupted synthesis.
clips.narration: On the leading-strand template, polymerase can follow the opening fork continuously. After a primer has provided a starting point, nucleotides are added one after another to make a single growing strand.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Lagging Strand, Okazaki Fragments, and Ligase
modules.description: The opposite template is copied discontinuously in fragments that are later joined by ligase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the lagging strand cannot be synthesized continuously.
Identify Okazaki fragments as short DNA segments on the lagging strand.
Describe DNA ligase as the enzyme that seals fragment junctions.
instructions: Compare the polymerase motion here with the leading-strand scene.
Watch fragment formation and then ligase sealing.

clips.changeMeaning: Polymerase is placed on the opposite template to set up the directional problem created by antiparallel DNA at the replication fork.
clips.narration: The second template presents a problem. Because polymerase can only synthesize 5-prime to 3-prime, it cannot simply follow the fork continuously on this strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Short daughter-strand segments appear while polymerase shifts position, showing repeated starts near the fork and growth away from it as Okazaki fragments.
clips.narration: Instead, polymerase works in short stretches. It starts near the fork, synthesizes a fragment away from the fork, then returns closer to the fork to begin again.

clips.changeMeaning: Ligase enters after fragment synthesis and the fragmented daughter strand is replaced by a sealed continuous strand to show successful junction repair.
clips.narration: These short pieces are called Okazaki fragments. DNA ligase seals the junctions between them, converting the discontinuous pieces into one continuous daughter strand.

modules.description: All major replication components operate together, linking antiparallel structure to leading- and lagging-strand asymmetry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase, SSBs, DNA polymerase, and ligase in one integrated fork.
Summarize the distinct functions of each replication component.
Relate leading and lagging asymmetry to antiparallel templates and 5' to 3' polymerase activity.
instructions: Survey the full fork and identify each labeled component.
Use the scene as an integrated review of the mechanism.

components.text:
Helicase: unwinds
SSBs: stabilize
Polymerase: synthesizes
Ligase: seals fragments

clips.changeMeaning: The entire fork is shown operating together with a summary panel so students can visually inventory all major components in one integrated mechanism.
clips.narration: Now the full replication fork is assembled. Helicase opens the DNA, single-strand binding proteins stabilize the templates, polymerases synthesize new DNA, and ligase seals the lagging-strand fragments.

clips.changeMeaning: The leading and lagging enzymes are advanced to contrast continuous versus discontinuous synthesis while linking the asymmetry back to strand orientation.
clips.narration: The key idea is that the two templates are antiparallel, but polymerase works only by extending DNA in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction. That is why one strand is made continuously and the other must be made in fragments.

modules.description: Students observe one and two rounds of replication to predict the composition of daughter molecules and explain why replication is semiconservative.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define semiconservative replication in terms of parental and newly synthesized strands.
Predict daughter-molecule composition after one round of replication.
Predict and verify the mixture of hybrid and fully new molecules after a second round.
instructions: Watch the first round, then pause mentally to predict the second round outcome.
Focus on the colors marking old and new strands.

components.text:
Predict round 2:
A) all 4 hybrid
B) 2 hybrid, 2 fully new
C) all 4 fully new

clips.changeMeaning: Two daughter molecules appear beside the parental DNA to illustrate the first replication outcome and establish the old-versus-new strand color coding.
clips.narration: After one round of replication, each daughter DNA molecule contains one original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. That is why DNA replication is called semiconservative.

clips.changeMeaning: A prediction panel appears before the second round so students must reason from the first-round products rather than only watching a provided answer.
clips.narration: Now predict the result after a second round of replication. Will all four molecules remain hybrid, will two stay hybrid while two become fully new, or will all four be fully new?

clips.changeMeaning: The four second-round products are revealed, with the first-round daughters shifted aside so the mixed set can be compared directly against the student's prediction.
clips.narration: The correct result is two hybrid molecules and two fully new molecules. Only molecules that inherit an original parental strand remain hybrid after the second round.

modules.description: A final summary scene reviews the six major concept areas covered across the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize DNA structure, pairing, directionality, enzyme action, strand asymmetry, and semiconservative replication.
Connect the earlier scenes into one coherent explanation of DNA replication.
Reinforce vocabulary and causal links among structure and mechanism.
instructions: Use this recap to consolidate the full sequence of ideas.
Listen for how each concept connects to the next.

components.text:
1) Double helix structure
2) Complementary base pairing

clips.changeMeaning: The recap board focuses first on structure and pairing so the review begins with foundational ideas before moving into replication mechanism.
clips.narration: First, remember the structure: two sugar-phosphate backbones form a double helix, and the bases pair specifically as A with T and G with C through hydrogen bonds.

components.text:
3) Antiparallel 5' and 3'
4) Helicase, SSBs, polymerase, ligase

clips.changeMeaning: The highlighted recap text updates to the next two themes, shifting from structural orientation into the coordinated actions of replication enzymes.
clips.narration: Next, the strands are antiparallel: one runs 5-prime to 3-prime and the other 3-prime to 5-prime. Replication then depends on helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase.

components.text:
5) Leading vs lagging strands
6) Semiconservative replication

clips.changeMeaning: The final recap highlight shifts to strand asymmetry and semiconservative outcomes, closing the conceptual chain from structure to daughter-molecule composition.
clips.narration: Because the templates are antiparallel and polymerase extends only 5-prime to 3-prime, DNA is copied with one leading strand and one lagging strand. The outcome is semiconservative replication, where each daughter molecule carries one old strand and one new strand.
